## Research question

Healthcare SQL systems must distinguish unsupported requests from answerable questions for which their generated query may still be unreliable.

## Method

QLoRA adapts SQLCoder-7b-2 for generation and answerability classification. Classifier training balances unanswerable questions against sampled answerable questions; a multitask variant combines classification and generation examples. A summed token-log-probability threshold and execution-error filter provide additional abstention decisions.

## Evaluation

The EHRSQL 2024 MIMIC-IV demo task has 5,124 training, 1,163 validation and 1,167 test questions. The paper reports incremental configurations and six confidence thresholds using penalty-dependent reliability scores. It explicitly chooses thresholds heuristically from the test-prediction score distribution.

## What the results support

The reported submission uses threshold −0.4 and ranks sixth, with RS(5) 55.27 and RS(10) 43.70. Different thresholds favor different penalties: −0.5 gives higher RS(5), while −0.2 gives RS(10) 43.87. Every reported RS(N) remains negative.

## Limits and qualifications

Test-score adaptation is not independent validation-set calibration; no test-label training is established. Raw sequence likelihood is not calibrated correctness and can depend on output length. Cascaded modules can wrongly reject valid queries or accept incorrect ones. Evaluation uses one benchmark setting without prospective clinical outcomes, external-hospital transfer or separate ambiguity resolution.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Core evidence for combining intrinsic answerability screening with candidate-level selective prediction. Successful SQL execution and high model likelihood do not establish that the request is answerable or the SQL semantically correct.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

Separately, generation can emit I do not know; execution errors and low sequence likelihood also yield null. These latter signals concern a particular model output and can occur for answerable questions. | Sections 4.2–4.4, pp. 699–700; pinned src/data_preparation/abstention_data_preparation.py lines 16–37 and 57–61; src/data_preparation/data_preparation.py lines 38–45; src/post_processing/post_processing.py lines 62–71 | Preserve the distinction between unsupported requests and unreliable candidate generation. A shared null output does not make their causes equivalent. |
| Confidence thresholds are calibrated on an independent validation set or prove a correctness probability. | Section 4.4.1 defines confidence as the sum of generated-token log probabilities and says that the threshold is chosen heuristically from the test-score distribution. Source sums scores without length normalization and reads test questions for inference; training preparation reads train labels only. | Figure 2 and Section 4.4.1, pp. 699–700; pinned src/finetuning/inference.py lines 37–43 and 79–86; src/post_processing/post_processing.py lines 39–51 | Describe adaptation to unlabeled test predictions, not independently calibrated risk. Empty result lists are serialized as results and are not rejected solely for emptiness. Section 6.1 acknowledges cascading errors, false acceptance and false rejection. No prospective clinician study, hospital-transfer evaluation or clinical patient-outcome assessment is reported. | Section 3, p. 698; Sections 5.2, 6.1 and 7, p. 701 | Limit the evidence to benchmark reliability under the described setup; neither a passing execution nor the reported leaderboard rank establishes clinical deployment safety. |
